title: Raga Tilang
hookLine: a raga with Persian color, where Guru Nanak speaks in words his Muslim neighbors used

cards: Yak araj guftam pes tu. Those are the first words under the heading Raga Tilang, on ang seven twenty-one of the Guru Granth Sahib. Say them aloud and they don't sound like the Punjabi of the hymns before them.
The words lean toward Persian, and a few lines later come names for God that Muslim neighbors in Guru Nanak's Punjab used. Same Guru, same book, same message, in a different set of clothes.
Today: Raga Tilang, and why a song might change its accent.

teach.b: Tilang follows little Bairari, and its section opens with Guru Nanak.

teach.h: ONE PLEA: LEND YOUR EAR, CREATOR.
teach.b: First, the plea, in plain English: I have made one petition before you; lend it your ear, Creator. Then the praise: you are true, great, generous, without flaw, the Sustainer. Then a hard turn.
The world is a place you pass through; know it for certain, heart. The angel of death has me by the hair, and the heart hasn't understood. Second, the color.
Listen to the names inside that praise: Karim, the generous one. Parvardigar, the one who sustains. Azrael, the angel of death.

These are Persian and Arabic words that Muslims in Punjab used. Some readers hear Tilang as a place where Guru Nanak speaks to Muslim listeners in their own words. He doesn't argue with their vocabulary.
He prays in it. The one God of the Granth's opening lines is still the one addressed; only the accent has changed, the way a good host greets a guest in the guest's language.
That's the persian color. Third, the ending, which needs no translation.

teach.h: THE DUST UNDER YOUR SERVANTS' FEET.
teach.b: Nanak says: your servant is the dust under the feet of your servants.
A petition that started by asking to be heard ends by asking to be low.

how: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Tilang section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Tilang, and listeners can hear in Guru Nanak's opening hymn the Persian and Arabic names for God, such as Karim and Parvardigar.

o: the raga of wedding songs and of funeral laments
a raga sung only in Persian at the royal courts
the raga after Bairari, opening with a Persian-colored plea

games.q: inside raga Tilang — tap the pairs.
p: the dust under the servants' feet

s: Tilang's opening hymn leans toward Persian words
it begins yak araj guftam pes tu, a petition to the Creator in Persian-colored speech.
in Tilang, Guru Nanak prays to a different God
the words change accent; the hymn still addresses the one Creator.
the hymn ends by asking to be seen as great
it ends with Nanak as the dust under the feet of God's servants.

games.q: you're singing to God, and some of your listeners use different words for the One than you do. what do you do?
o: stick to your own words so nobody gets confused.
pray in their words, to the same One.
skip the names and just sing the tune.
games.why: in Tilang, Guru Nanak's plea leans toward Persian and calls God Karim and Parvardigar. the accent changes; the One addressed doesn't.

practice: If you'd like, play a shabad in Raga Tilang, or bring to mind one person whose words for the deepest things differ from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a grandparent.
Don't translate them; just hear them the way they'd say it, and let those words be welcome beside your breath, with one soft Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Raga Tilang. The raga after Bairari, where Guru Nanak's opening plea leans toward Persian and calls God Karim and Parvardigar. Today's word.

orig.note: tilang, the raga that follows Bairari in the Guru Granth Sahib, opening with a Persian-colored plea.

carryVoice: Your line: persian color. Not a different faith, a different set of words reaching for the same One. A week done.
